title: CHAPTER 2: OFFICIAL LANGUAGES ACT, 1963 AND RULES, 1976

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The Official Languages Act was enacted in 1963 to provide for the languages used for official purposes of the Union.
The Official Languages Rules were framed in 1976 under Section 8 of the 1963 Act to regulate language implementation.
For official communications, India is classified into three distinct zones: Region A, Region B, and Region C.

blocks.content: As per Article 343(3) of the Constitution, Parliament passed the Official Languages Act, 1963 to provide for continued use of English even after 15 years (January 26, 1965). It also made provisions for the use of Hindi and English in official communications. This Act was amended in 1967 to make certain provisions more specific.

cells: 'Central Government Offices' means Ministries, Departments, Secretariats, and offices of Central Government
English to continue to be used for all official purposes of the Union for which it was being used immediately before 26 January 1965 (i.e., indefinitely unless Parliament decides otherwise)
All bills, acts, ordinances, orders, bye-laws, rules, regulations, notifications :shall be in both Hindi and English; English text shall be authoritative
If resolution passed in both houses must be in both languages; communication between Union and non-Hindi state :in English
No provision in this Act shall derogate from rights of persons belonging to linguistic minorities; each person may use mother tongue for official communications
Union shall promote and use Hindi and Devanagari numerals in official work; this is directive
Committee of Parliament to be constituted to review progress in use of Hindi; submit report to President; recommend steps
Optional use of Hindi by a State
Governor of a State may with consent of President direct use of Hindi/State official language in communications with that state
Provisions about mandatory Hindi do not apply to communications with non-Hindi states; English to be used there
Article 348 provides English in HCs; this section cross-references
No person shall be discriminated in employment by reason only that they are not proficient in Hindi

rows: States and UTs where Hindi is the primary language of communication (e.g., UP, MP, Bihar, Rajasthan, Haryana, Delhi).
States and UTs where communication with the Union is substantially in Hindi (e.g., Maharashtra, Gujarat, Punjab, Chandigarh).
All other States and Union Territories not included in Region A or Region B (e.g., Southern States, North-Eastern States).

blocks.content: The Official Languages Rules were framed in 1976 under Section 8(1) of the Official Languages Act, 1963. They lay down specific rules for the use of Hindi and English in official work of Central Government offices. These rules are the practical framework for implementing Hindi in day-to-day official work.

cells: Minutes and proceedings of all meetings and resolutions shall be in Hindi or English or both; meetings normally in Hindi in Region A offices

Communications between Region A offices :Hindi; Region A to Region B :Hindi with English translation; Region A/B to Region C :English; communication between any two offices :either can use the language of their region
Communications to States in Region A :in Hindi; States in Region B :in Hindi with English translation if requested; States in Region C :in English
With persons in Region A/B :Hindi; Region C :English; persons can request English even in Region A
Where English text prepared for certain purposes, Hindi version shall also be prepared simultaneously
If employee submits application in Hindi, it shall be replied in Hindi; same for English application
Head of office shall identify employees who have adequate knowledge of Hindi; maintain record
Hindi training shall be arranged; incentives for learning Hindi; books and materials in Hindi to be provided
All correspondence in Hindi shall be in Devanagari script only; not Roman Hindi
Arrangements for inspection of offices for compliance with these rules; periodic review by Department of Official Language

blocks.content: 2.3 Region A, B, and C Classification

items: Memorize the distinction between Region A, Region B, and Region C as it is frequently tested in Official Language (Rajbhasha) exam sections.
Note the exact years of enactment: Official Languages Act (1963) vs. Official Languages Rules (1976).

cells: Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand, Bihar, Jharkhand, Rajasthan, Himachal Pradesh, Haryana, Delhi, Andaman and Nicobar Islands (Central Secretariat)
All inter-office communications in Hindi; percentage targets very high (100% in some categories)
Maharashtra, Gujarat, Punjab (partially), Chandigarh, Goa, Odisha, West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Manipur, Tripura, Mizoram, Nagaland, Arunachal Pradesh, Sikkim, Jammu & Kashmir (approx.)
Communications in Hindi with English translation provided; gradual increase in Hindi use; moderately high targets
Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka, Andaman & Nicobar Islands (for external correspondence), Lakshadweep, Pondicherry, Daman & Diu, Dadra & Nagar Haveli
Communications in English (or English with Hindi translation if recipient requests); lower Hindi targets

blocks.content: Important: A bank's communication language depends on its Region classification. RRBs operating in Region A states must achieve higher Hindi targets. All Central Government offices (including nationalised banks) are covered.
